title: Manning's equation: sizing a channel from slope, roughness and shape

explain.say: In eighteen eighty nine the Irish engineer Robert Manning presented a simple formula that engineers still use every day to size canals, drains and culverts. It links speed to slope, roughness and shape. On the board, two channels of the same shape: one lined with smooth concrete, one with grass.

draw.text: Manning's equation: sizing a channel from slope, roughness and shape

curves.label: Grassy n = 0.030
curves.ask: What is Manning's roughness coefficient n?

marks.label: S = 1 in 1000
marks.ask: How do you calculate the flow in a channel?

explain.say: Look at the concrete curve. Velocity equals one over n, times R to the power two thirds, times the square root of the slope S. Here n is the roughness, about zero point zero one five for concrete. R is the hydraulic radius: the flow area divided by the wetted perimeter, the length of channel the water touches. Steeper slope, faster water, but only as the square root.

marks.ask: How do you calculate the flow in a channel?

explain.say: Let us try a channel three metres wide with water one metre deep. The area is three square metres; the wetted perimeter is one plus three plus one, five metres; so R is zero point six. At a slope of one in a thousand, V is one over zero point zero one five, times zero point seven one one, times zero point zero three one six: about one point five metres per second.

explain.say: Now the grassy channel, with n of zero point zero three. Twice as rough, so at the same slope it flows at half the speed, about zero point seven five metres per second, and carries half the flow. To carry as much it must be bigger. Which lining would you choose for a city storm drain?

explain.say: Concrete, to move water fast! Choosing n is the art. Smooth pipes are near zero point zero one, clean earth canals near zero point zero two five, weedy rivers zero point zero five, and a wooded floodplain can reach zero point one. Great work! Challenge: if you doubled the slope of the concrete channel, how much faster would it flow?

faq.a: It gives the average velocity of uniform flow in a channel: V equals one over n times R to the two thirds times S to the half. Multiply by the flow area to get the discharge.

faq.q: What is Manning's roughness coefficient n?
faq.a: n describes how rough the channel lining is. Smooth PVC is about 0.009, finished concrete about 0.013 to 0.015, earth canals about 0.025 and weedy rivers 0.05 or more.
Hydraulic radius is the flow area divided by the wetted perimeter. For a channel 3 metres wide and 1 metre deep, it is 3 over 5, which is 0.6 metres.

faq.q: How do you calculate the flow in a channel?
faq.a: Find the area and wetted perimeter, work out R, use Manning to get the velocity, then multiply by the area. Our concrete channel carries 1.5 times 3, about 4.5 cubic metres per second.

faq.q: Why does doubling the slope not double the speed?
faq.a: Velocity depends on the square root of the slope, so doubling the slope multiplies the speed by the square root of 2, about 1.41.

facts: Robert Manning presented his flow formula to the Institution of Civil Engineers of Ireland in 1889.
For a wide, shallow channel, the hydraulic radius is close to the flow depth.
